front.title: The Incident Detection Message Exchange Format version 2 (IDMEFv2)

abstract.t: The Incident Detection Message Exchange Format version 2 (IDMEFv2) defines a data representation for security incidents detected on cyber and/or physical infrastructures.

The format is agnostic so it can be used in standalone or combined cyber (SIEM), physical (PSIM) and availability (NMS) monitoring systems. IDMEFv2 can also be used to represent man made or natural hazards threats.

IDMEFv2 improves situational awareness by facilitating correlation of multiple types of events using the same base format thus enabling efficient detection of complex and combined cyber and physical attacks and incidents.
This draft is maintained by the IDMEFv2 Task Force. Please consult our website for more information: https://www.idmefv2.org.
If approved this draft will obsolete RFC4765.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The Incident Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) is intended to solve the problem of security monitoring compartmentalization by proposing a single format to represent any type of incident, whether cyber or physical, intentional or accidental, natural or man-made.
Indeed security is often associated to the Confidentiality-Integrity-Availability triad, performance and availability management systems are still run independently from security management systems.

Additionally, with the adoption and integration of Internet of Things (IoT) and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices, and the exponential emergence of smart systems (transport, cities, buildings, etc), an increasingly interconnected mesh of cyber-physical systems (CPS) has emerged. This expansion of the attack and incident surfaces blurs the once-clear functions of cybersecurity and physical security.
Finally, as IT infrastructure moves out of data centers it becomes more exposed to external threats, including natural and man-made hazards.

Incident detection systems have traditionally focused on detecting cyber incidents or physical incident or availability incidents. There is an increasing need nowadays to have a unified view and management of all those incidents and their interconnection.
To achieve this goal the Incident Detection Message Exchange Format offers a unique data representation for multiple types of events:

li.t: Cyber-security events (e.g. authentication failure/success, virus/malware detection, bruteforce/scan detection, etc.)
Physical security events (e.g. intrusion detection, object detection, face or activity recognition, fire/smoke/noise/rain detection, etc.)
Availability/observability/performance events (e.g. system failure, service malfunction, performance decrease, etc.)
Natural and man made hazards events (e.g. wildfires, avalanches, droughts, earthquakes, pollution, fire, explosion, etc.)

section.name: IDMEFv2 deployment architecture
section.t: IDMEFv2 can be used to exchange incident detection information between specialized managers (SIEM, PSIM, NMS) and a universal "Cyber & Physical SIEM" (CPSIEM) or directly from specialized analyzers and a CPSIEM.
IDMEFv2 improves situational awareness by enabling correlation of multiple types of events using the same base format.
This document defines a model serialization methods for the purpose of describing and sharing these events.

section.name: IDMEFv1 (Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format) - RFC 4765 - Legacy
section.t: IDMEFv2 (Incident Detection Message Exchange Format) is based on IDMEFv1 (Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format) concepts. But IDMEFv1 was cyber intrusion focused as IDMEFv2 perimeter is much larger. Thus retro-compatibility although partly possible has not been a priority.

section.name: Relationship between IDMEFv2 and other event/incident formats
section.t: IDMEFv2 focuses essentialy on high level event/incident correlation and detection.There are many standard and proprietary formats on the incident detection market and in particular on the cybersecurity market. IDMEFv2 is complementary to most of these formats.
IDMEFv1 (Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format - RFC 4765) : IDMEFv2 (Incident Detection) replaces and obsoletes IDMEFv1 (Intrusion Detection) by covering a wider spectrum.

IODEFv2 (Incident Object Definition Exchange Format - RFC 5070) : IDMEFv2 helps detect incident. When an incident is detected it will be analysed and eventually fully described and shared with other security teams through IODEFv2. IDMEF is used upstream IODEFv2. IDMEFv2 alerts can be “attached” to IODEFv2 object to provide technical details about incidents.

Syslog (System Logging) : Syslog is a lossy format with no formal structure. Syslog can be used by sensors to send information to analyzers. Out of those multi-format syslogs the analyzer might detect an incident or an event of interest. The analyzer will then use IDMEFv2 to notify the manager which might correlate this information with other data to confirm the incident.

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) : SNMP polls information from devices which is then compared to thresholds to detect incident. IDMEFv2 can be used when incident is detected downstream of SNMP to communicate the incident to the manager. IDMEFv2 can have a similar role as SNMP Traps.

STIX (Structured Threat Information Expression) : is a language and serialization format used to exchange cyber threat intelligence (CTI). IDMEFv2 can help detect incidents which might lead to the creation and sharing of STIX information. Cyber analyzer can also rely on STIX information to detect incidents that will be notified in IDMEFv2 format.

OCSF (The Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework) is an open-source, vendor-agnostic standard designed to normalize security telemetry from diverse tools. It provides a common language and consistent structure for security event data, simplifying data ingestion, correlation, and analysis. OCSF can be seen as a “super” syslog to describe events before IDMEFv2 extract “incidents”. OCSF is limited to cyber security.

SIEM proprietory formats (CEF, LEEF, ECS, CIM, ...) : By covering cyber, physical and monitoring incidents type, IDMEFv2 offers a wider spectrum than those formats. Gateways between IDMEFv2 and those formats can be developped to connect legacy cyber detection systems to an IDMEFv2 architecture.

section.name: Existing Deployments and Adoption
section.t: IDMEFv2 is not a theoretical proposal. It has been developed, validated, and deployed within the framework of eight large-scale European research projects, funded by the Horizon 2020 and Digital Europe programmes. These projects — namely 7SHIELD, PRECINCT, CyberSEAS, ATLANTIS, ENDURANCE, KINAITICS, TESTUDO, and SAFE4SOC — address critical sectors such as space systems, energy grids, transportation, and government infrastructure. These implementations span multiple domains, including Security Operations Centers (SOCs), Physical Security Information Management (PSIM) systems, and critical infrastructure protection pilots.

This document aims to formalize this existing practice as an IETF Experimental RFC, to ensure interoperability, gather broader community feedback, and provide a stable foundation for future developments.

section.name: Event
section.t: An event is something that triggered a notice. Any incident starts off as an event or a combination of events, but not all events result in an incident. An event does not need be an indication of wrongdoing. E.g. someone successfully logging in or entering a building is an event.

section.name: Incident
section.t: An incident is an event that compromises or has a significant probability of compromising at least one of the organization's security criteria such as Confidentiality, Integrity or Availability. An incident may affect a production tool, personnel, etc. It may be logical, physical or organizational in nature. Last but not least, an incident may be caused on purpose or by accident.

section.name: Alert
section.t: An alert is a notification/message that a particular event/incident (or series of events/incidents) has occurred.

section.name: Manager
section.t: The manager is the central console toward which all analyzers send their alerts. The manager collects, correlates, stores and displays the alerts to the operators.

Example : - A SIEM (Security Information & Event Management) or a Log Manager) - A PSIM (Physical Security Information Management) - A NMS (Network Management System) - A CPSIEM (Cyber & Physical Security Information Management System)

section.name: Operator
section.t: The level 1 operator is in charge of receiving manager notifications and identify or confirm when an event should be considered as an incident. The operator must also decide if there is a known resolution for this incident or if it needs a deeper analysys.

section.name: Analyst
section.t: The analyst will be contacted by the operator to analyze complex incidents that can’t be easily resolved. The investigation starts with the IDMEFv2 information but the analyst might need more information like raw logs for a deeper forensics.

section.name: Attack
section.t: An attack is an attempt to destroy, expose, alter, disable, steal or gain unauthorized access to or make unauthorized use of a cyber or physical asset. An attack is one or many kinds of incidents.

section.name: Correlation
section.t: Correlation is the identification of relationships between two or more events.

section.name: Aggregation
section.t: Aggregation is the consolidation of similar events into a single event.

section.name: The IDMEF Data Types
section.t: Each object inside the IDMEF data model has an associated data type. This type may be used to validate the content of incoming IDMEF messages.

section.name: Classes
section.t: The classes are meant to group related attributes together. Some of the classes may be instanciated multiple times (e.g. Source, Target, etc.) while others may only appear once in an IDMEF message (e.g. Analyzer).

section.name: Integers
section.t: Integers inside the IDMEF data model are expressed using the following ABNF grammar:
section.sourcecode: integer = *1minus int int = zero / ( digit1-9 *DIGIT ) minus = %x2D ; - zero = %0x30 ; 0 digit1-9 = %x31-39 ; 1-9
section.t: Such values are indicated with the "INT" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Floating-point values
section.t: Floating-point values inside the IDMEF data model are expressed using the following ABNF grammar:
This grammar reuses some of the production rules listed in .
Such values are indicated with the "FLOAT" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Strings
section.t: Strings are series of characters from the standard and are used to represent a text.
For readability, this document uses quotes (") to delimit strings, but please note that these quotes are not syntactically part of the actual strings.
E.g. "Hello world".
Some of the strings used in the IDMEFv2 data model follow a stricter syntax. These are included below for completeness.
Such values are indicated with the "STRING" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Enumerations
section.t: Enumerations are special strings used when valid values for an IDMEF attribute are restricted to those present in a predefined list.
Such values are indicated with the "ENUM" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Timestamps
section.t: Timestamps are used to indicate a specific moment in time. The timestamps used in the IDMEF data model follow the syntax defined by the "date-time" production rule of the grammar in ch 5.6.
E.g. "1985-04-12T23:59:59.52Z" represents a moment just before April 5th, 1985 in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
Such values are indicated with the "TIMESTAMP" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Geographical Locations
section.t: Some attributes inside the IDMEF data model may refer to geographical locations using a set of coordinates. The reference system for all geographical coordinates is a geographic coordinate reference system, using the World Geodetic System 1984 . The reference system used is the same as for the Global Positioning System (GPS).

The format for such values can be either "latitude,longitude" or "latitude,longitude,altitude". Each of these coordinates is represented as a floating-point value. The latitude and longitude are expressed in degrees while the altitude is expressed in meters.

E.g. "48.8584,2.2945,276.13" matches the (3-dimensional) geographical location for the top floor or the Eiffel Tower located in Paris, France, while "48.8584,2.2945" matches the same location in two dimensions (with the altitude removed).
Such values are indicated with the "GEOLOC" type annotation in the model.

section.name: UNECE Location Codes (UN/LOCODE)
section.t: Some attributes inside the IDMEF data model may refer to geographical locations using Locations Codes. These codes can be assimilated to an enumeration, where the list of possible values is defined in the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) Codes for Trade .
E.g. "FR PAR" is the Location Code for the city of Paris, France.
Such values are indicated with the "UNLOCODE" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
section.t: The IDMEF data model uses Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs), as defined in , when referring to external resources. Unless otherwise specified, either a Uniform Resource Location (URL) or a Uniform Resource Name (URN) may be used where a URI is expected.
E.g. both "https://example.com/resource" and "urn:myapp:resource" are valid Uniform Resource Identifiers.
Such values are indicated with the "URI" type annotation in the model.

section.name: IP Addresses
section.t: IP addresses inside the IDMEF data model are expressed as strings using the traditional dotted-decimal notation for IPv4 addresses (defined by the "dotnum" production rule in the grammar in ), while IPv6 addresses are expressed using the text representation defined in ch 2.2.
E.g. "192.0.2.1" represents a valid IPv4 address, while "::1/128" represents a valid IPv6 address.
It is RECOMMENDED that implementations follow the recommendations for IPv6 text representation stated in .
Such values are indicated with the "IP" type annotation in the model.

section.name: E-mail addresses
section.t: E-mail addresses inside the IDMEF data model are expressed as strings using the address specification syntax defined in ch 3.4.1.
E.g. "root@example.com".
Such values are indicated with the "EMAIL" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Attachment names
section.t: Attachments inside the IDMEF data model are identified using a unique name, composed of a string whose character set is limited to the ASCII letters (A-Z a-z) and digits (0-9).
E.g. "state" is a valid name for an attachment.
The constraint on name unicity is enforced per class. That is, but it is not possible for two attachments to share the same name inside the same alert.
Such values are indicated with the "ID" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Media types
section.t: Media types are used in the IDMEF data model to describe an attachment's content. The syntax for such values is defined in .
IANA keeps a list of all currently registered media types in the Media Types registry .
E.g. "application/xml" or "text/plain; charset=utf-8".
Such values are indicated with the "MEDIATYPE" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)
section.t: Universally Unique Identifiers (UUIDs) are used to uniquely identify IDMEF messages. It is also possible for an IDMEF message to reference other IDMEF messages using their UUIDs. The syntax for UUIDs is defined in .
To limit the risk of UUID collisions, implementors SHOULD NOT generate version 4 UUIDs (randomly or pseudo-randomly generated UUIDs).
UUIDs are case-insensitive when used in comparisons.
Such values are indicated with the "UUID" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Protocol Names
section.t: Such values are indicated with the "PROTOCOL" type annotation in the model.

section.name: IDMEF Paths
section.t: This document defines a way to represent the path to every possible attribute inside an IDMEF message. For conciseness, the top-level "Alert" class is omitted from the path.

This representation can be used in contexts where the path to an IDMEF attribute is expected. An example of such usage can be seen in the definition of the "AggrCondition" attribute inside the Alert class.
The syntax for these IDMEF paths is expressed in the following ABNF grammar:
section.sourcecode: class-name = "Analyzer" / "Sensor" / "Source" / "Target" / "Attachment" attribute-name = 1*ALPHA class-reference = class-name "." num = *1"-" 1*DIGIT list-index = "(" num ")" path = *1class-reference attribute-name *1list-index
section.t: Valid attribute names are limited to those defined for the specified class-reference (or in the top-level "Alert" class if class-reference is omitted).
For example, the following path refers to the "CeaseTime" attribute of the top-level "Alert" class: "CeaseTime".
Likewise, the following path refers to the "Name" attribute of the "Analyzer" class: "Analyzer.Name".

For attributes defined as lists (see ), the path may include the (0-based) index for an entry inside the list. The index defaults to 0 if omitted. This means that several (valid) representations may be used to reference the same IDMEF attribute when list attributes are involved.

Compatible implementations MUST reject paths that reference an unknown class, an unknown attribute, or use a list-index for an IDMEF field which is not defined as a list.
A compatible implementation MUST also normalize paths before comparing them (e.g. by stripping the text "(0)" from paths referring to list attributes).

section.name: Hashes
section.t: Hashes are sometimes used inside the data model to protect the integrity (and optionally, authenticity) of attachments.

The syntax for these values is "function:hash_result", where "function" refers to one of the hashing function names listed in and "hash_result" contains the hexadecimal notation for the hash result obtained by calling the specified hash function on the input value.
In the context of IDMEF, either a keyless or keyed hash function may be used to process the raw input value.
Hashes are case-insensitive when used in comparisons.
Such values are indicated with the "HASH" type annotation in the model.

section.name: Lists
section.t: Some attributes of the IDMEF data model accept ordered lists of values.

Such ordered lists are indicated with the "X[]" type annotation in the model. where "X" refers to one of the data types defined in . For example, "ENUM[]" refers to an ordered list of enumeration values.

section.name: The IDMEF extension
section.t: In order to support the dynamic nature of security operations and to adapt to specific needs, the IDMEFv2 data model will need to continue to evolve. This section discusses how new data elements can be incorporated into the IDMEFv2. There is support to add additional enumerated values and new attributes.

These extension mechanisms are designed so that adding new data elements is possible without requiring modifications to this document. Extensions can be implemented publicly or privately. With proven value, well-documented extensions can be incorporated into future versions of the specification.

section.name: Extending the Enumerated Values of Attributes
section.t: Additional enumerated values can be added to select attributes either through the use of specially marked attributes with the "ext-" prefix or through a set of corresponding IANA registries. The former approach allows for the extension to remain private. The latter approach is public.

section.name: Private Extension of Enumerated Values
section.t: The data model supports adding new enumerated values to an attribute without public registration. For each attribute that supports this extension technique, there is a corresponding attribute in the same element whose name is identical but with a prefix of "ext-". This special attribute is referred to as the extension attribute. The attribute being extended is referred to as an extensible attribute. For example, an extensible attribute named "foo" will have a corresponding extension attribute named "ext-foo". An element may have many extensible attributes.

In addition to a corresponding extension attribute, each extensible attribute has "ext-value" as one its possible enumerated values. Selection of this particular value in an extensible attribute signals that the extension attribute contains data. Otherwise, this "ext-value" value has no meaning.

In order to add a new enumerated value to an extensible attribute, the value of this attribute MUST be set to "ext-value", and the new desired value MUST be set in the corresponding extension attribute. For example, extending the Category attribute of the Analyzer class would look as follows:

section.t: The data model also supports publicly extending select enumerated attributes. A new entry can be added by registering a new entry in the appropriate IANA registry. Section () provides a mapping between the extensible attributes and their corresponding registry.

section.name: The IDMEF Data Model
section.t: In this section, the individual components of the IDMEF data model will be discussed in detail. For each class, the semantics will be described.

section.name: Overview
section.t: An IDMEF message is composed of an instance of the Alert class representing the overall properties of the message. It also contains exactly one instance of the Analyzer class and zero or more instances of the Sensor class. The message may also describe various aspects of an event using the Source and Target classes.
Last but not least, it may also include zero or more instances of the Attachment class, e.g. captured files or network packets related to the event for example.
The relationship between the main Alert class and other classes of the data model is shown in (attributes are omitted for clarity).

It is important to note that the data model does not specify how an incident should be categorized or identified. For example, an attacker scanning a network for machines listening on a specific port may be identified by one analyzer as a single attack against multiple targets, while another analyzer may identify it as multiple attacks from a single source. However, once an analyzer has determined the type of alert it plans on sending, the data model dictates how that alert should be formatted.

section.name: The Alert Class
section.t: The Alert class contains high level information about the event that triggered the alert.

figure.name: The Alert class
figure.artwork: +------------------------------+ | Alert | +------------------------------+ | STRING Version | | UUID ID | | STRING OrganisationName | | STRING OrganisationId | | STRING EntityName | | STRING EntityId | | ENUM[] EntitySector | | ENUM[] Type | | ENUM[] Category | | STRING[] ext-Category | | ENUM Cause | | STRING Description | | ENUM[] Status | | ENUM Priority | | FLOAT Confidence | | STRING Note | | TIMESTAMP CreateTime | | TIMESTAMP StartTime | | TIMESTAMP EndTime | | TIMESTAMP ReportTime | | STRING[] AltNames | | STRING[] AltCategory | | URI[] Ref | | UUID[] CorrelID | | CONDITION[] AggrCondition | | UUID[] PredID | | UUID[] RelID | | STRING[] SignedAttributes | | STRING Signature | +------------------------------+

section.t: The aggregate classes that make up Alert are:

dd.t: Exactly one. An instance of the Analyzer class that describes the tool/device responsible for the analysis that resulted in the alert being created and sent.
Zero or more. Instances of the Sensor class used to describe the sensor(s) that captured the information used during the analysis.

Depending on the tools/devices used to detect incidents, an Analyzer may rely on the output from a single sensor or from multiple sensors to generate alerts. In addition, the Analyzer and Sensor may actually be part of the same physical device and may share some of their attributes (e.g. IP, Hostname, Model, etc.).
Zero or more. Instances of the Source class used to describe the source(s) of the incident (e.g. attackers, faulty device, etc.).
Zero or more. Instances of the Target class used to describe the target(s) of the incident, i.e. the impacted devices/users/services/locations.
Zero or more. Instances of the Attachment class used to describe the electronic artifacts captured in relation with the event.

The intent of the Attachment class is to keep track of the electronic files left as a trail during the event. This may include things like on-disk files (e.g. malware samples), network packet captures, videos or still images from a camera feed, voice recording, etc.

section.t: The Alert class has the following attributes:

dd.t: Mandatory. The version of the IDMEF format in use by this alert.
During the drafts tuning period the version is equal to the draft version. Therefore it is "2.D.V0X" for Draft V0X.
Mandatory. Unique identifier for the alert.
Optional. Corporate/Main Office Organisation Name
Useful if alerts are sent to a multi-organisation central incident detection manager.
Example: ACME Corporation
Optional. Corporate/Main Office Organisation ID. Where possible official organisation ID manage by national authority.
Useful if alerts are sent to a multi-organisation central incident detection manager.
This ID has to be chosen depending on the overall detection perimeter and the nature of the monitored organisation (Private/Public, Commercial, International, etc.)

Examples: OrganisationId in France could be SIREN, in England could be CR, Germany could be Handelsregisternummer, Spain could be CIF, Italia could be Partita IVA, USA could be EIN, etc. Commercial OrganisationId in Europe could be V.A.T ID
Optional. Entity Name, monitored by the organisation, where the incident occurred.
Could be a town, region or country name or an internal name. Could also be the name of a customer for a MSSP centralizing it's customer incidents in a single system.
Do not repeat the organisation name in the EntityName
Example:
- ACME HeadQuaters is located in Paris France and has a local office in India
- If the incident occurred in the local office: "OrganisationName": "ACME" , "EntityName": "India"
- If the incident occurred in the headquaters: "OrganisationName": "ACME", "EntityName": "Headquaters" (or "Paris")
Optional. Entity ID, monitored by the organisation, where the incident occurred.
Useful if organisation and entity are not directly linked, like a customer and a MSSP.

Optional. The economic sector(s) and sub-sector(s) in which the entity operates. Values follow the dot notation sector.subsector based on the critical infrastructure taxonomy defined in the NIS2 Directive and CER (Critical Entities Resilience) Directive.
This attribute enables sector-based correlation, regulatory compliance reporting, and risk context for incident detection.
Enumeration available here
Optional. Incident type.

td.t: Incident involving cyberspace, information systems, or digital assets.
Incident involving physical assets, facilities, or infrastructure.
Incident affecting the availability or performance of a service, system, asset or resource.
Incident arising from natural, societal, technological, environmental, or other hazards.
Incident involving two or more incident types.

dd.t: Optional. Incident category.
Enumeration available here
Optional. A means by which to extend the Category attribute. (see )

Optional. Incident cause. The cause can be modified by any analyzer on the way of the alert and later by the operator and/or the analyst if new investigation reveals and confirms a different cause of the event.

td.t: The event is related to an expected phenomenon or to a phenomenon that does not qualify as out of the ordinary.
The event is related to a human error.
The event is related to malicious code or malicious actions.
The event is related to a device or service malfunction.
The event is related to a hazard phenomenon.
The cause of the event is unknown.

dd.t: Optional. Short free text human-readable description of the event. The description can add detail to the event category for easiest/faster comprehension by the operator. Example : * Cryptoware WannaCry blocked on pegasus server * Unknown person entering through east doorway
Optional. Event state in the overall event lifecycle.

td.t: The event is still considered as an harmless event and should not be treated.
The event is considered as an incident and should be taken care of.
The incident is confirmed and actively being investigated.
Investigation is finished and the issue is handled.
Investigation is finished, incident was a false positive.
Incident is obsolete, usually by another incident.

dd.t: Optional. Priority of the alert. Priority is defined by combining impact and urgency. It indicates how fast the incident should be taken care of.

td.t: Informational event with no current impact; no action or follow-up is required.
Minor incident with negligible impact; a workaround exists, and resolution can be scheduled.
Moderate incident affecting a limited scope; requires timely attention but is not immediately business-threatening.
Significant incident with major service degradation or impact on important assets; demands an urgent response.
Severe incident with business-critical systems down or vital interests threatened; requires immediate action and escalation.

dd.t: Optional. A floating-point value between 0 and 1 indicating the analyzer's confidence in its own reliability of this particular detection, where 0 means that the detection is surely incorrect while 1 means there is no doubt about the detection made.
Optional. Free text human-readable additional note, possibly a longer description of the incident if is not already obvious.

The Note attribute can be used to store any additional information. It can be additional information about the event and/or about the incident resolution, although the incident resolution information should in principle be stored elsewhere (with a link with the external tool in AltNames)
Mandatory. Timestamp indicating when the alert was created.
Optional. Timestamp indicating the deduced start of the event.
StartTime can be later than CreateTime in case or Alerts created from forecast information (e.g. Snow Storm expected in two days staring at 10h00)
Optional. Timestamp indicating the deduced end of the event.
Optional. Timestamp indicating the reporting time of the event, usually to an external CSIRT or a central SIEM.
Optional. Alternative identifiers; strings which help pair the event to internal systems' information (for example ticket IDs inside a request tracking systems).
Optional. Alternate categories from a reference other than IDMEFv2 categories (e.g. MISP, MITRE ATT@CK or another proprietary/internal reference).
Optional. References to sources of information related to the incident and/or vulnerability, and specific to this incident.
This MAY be a URL to additional info, or a URN in a registered or unregistered ad-hoc namespace bearing reasonable information value and uniqueness, such as "urn:cve:CVE-2013-2266".
Optional. Identifiers for the messages which were used as information sources to create this message, in case the message has been created based on correlation/analysis/deduction from other messages.
Optional. A list of IDMEF fields used to aggregate events. The values for these fields will be the same in all aggregated events.
This attribute should mostly be set by intermediary nodes, which detect duplicates, or aggregate events, spanning multiple detection windows, into a longer one.
The "StartTime" and "EndTime" attributes are used in conjunction with this attribute to describe the aggregation window.
Optional. A list containing the identifiers of previous messages which are obsoleted by this message.
The obsoleted alerts SHOULD NOT be used anymore. This field can be used to "update" an alert.
Optional. A list containing the identifiers of other messages related to this message.
Optional. List of IDMEFv2 paths of the attributes included in the signature.
Optional. JWS Compact Serialization string containing the signature.

section.name: The Analyzer Class
section.t: The Analyzer class describes the module that has analyzed the data captured by the sensors, identified an event of interest and decided to create an alert.

figure.artwork: +-----------------------+ | Analyzer | +-----------------------+ | UUID ID | | IP IP | | STRING Name | | STRING Hostname | | STRING Model | | ENUM[] Category | | STRING[] ext-Category | | ENUM[] Data | | STRING[] ext-Data | | ENUM[] Method | | STRING[] ext-Method | | GEOLOC GeoLocation | | UNLOCODE UnLocation | | STRING Location | | STRING Locator | | STRING CaptureZone | +-----------------------+

section.t: The Analyzer class has the following attributes:

dd.t: Optional. Unique identifier for the analyzer.
Optional. Analyzer IP address.
Recommended. Name of the analyzer, which must be reasonably unique, however still bear some meaningful sense.
This attribute usually denotes the hierarchy of organizational units the detector belongs to and its own name. It MAY also be used to distinguish multiple analyzers running with the same IP address.
Optional. Hostname of this analyzer.

section.name: The JavaScript Object Notation Serialization Method
section.t: This serialization method aims to convert IDMEFv2 messages to a format that is easy to parse and process, both by software/hardware processors, as well as humans. It relies on the the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format defined in [RFC8259].
Conforming implementations MUST implement all the requirements specified in [RFC8259].
In addition, the following rules MUST be observed when serializing an IDMEFv2 message:

li.t: The top-level Alert class (Section 5.2) is represented as a JSON object ([RFC8259]). This JSON object is returned to the calling process at the end of the serialization process.

Aggregate classes are represented as JSON objects and stored as members of the top-level JSON object, using the same name as in the IDMEF data model. E.g. the appears under the name "Analyzer" inside the top-level JSON object.

Attributes are stored as members of the JSON object representing the class they belong to, using the same name as in the IDMEF data model. E.g. the "Version" attribute from the is stored under the name "Version" inside the top-level JSON object.

Lists from the IDMEF data model are represented as JSON arrays ([RFC8259]). This also applies to aggregate classes where a list is expected. E.g. the "Sensor" member inside the top-level JSON object contains a list of objects, where each object represents an instance of the .
The various string-based data types listed in Section 3 are represented as JSON strings ([RFC8259]). Please note that the issues outlined in [RFC8259] regarding strings processing also apply here.
IDMEF attributes with the "NUMBER" data type are represented as JSON numbers ([RFC8259]).

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document describes a data representation for exchanging security-related information between incident detection system implementations. Although there are no security concerns directly applicable to the format of this data, the data itself may contain security-sensitive information whose confidentiality, integrity, and/or availability may need to be protected.

This suggests that the systems used to collect, transmit, process, and store this data should be protected against unauthorized use and that the data itself should be protected against unauthorized access.

The underlying messaging format and protocol used to exchange instances of the IDMEF MUST provide appropriate guarantees of confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. The use of a standardized security protocol is encouraged.
The draft-lehmann-idmefv2-https-transport-01.txt document defines the transportation of IDMEF over HTTPs that provides such security.

October 2026

section.name: The Dynamic Asset Problem
section.t: Modern container orchestration platforms and cloud runtime environments create and terminate resources dynamically. IP addresses may change or be reassigned, resource names may be reused, and an entity involved in a security incident may no longer exist when an investigation takes place.
Consequently, identifying a resource solely by its IP address or hostname is insufficient for reliable incident correlation and post-incident investigation.

IDMEFv2 provides complementary attributes that can describe dynamic entities in the , , , and classes. The attribute identifies an entity in the IDMEFv2 data model, while , , and provide additional information about its network presence, operational hostname, and infrastructure context.

These attributes serve different purposes and SHOULD be used together when the relevant information is available. They do not, by themselves, guarantee the long-term availability of historical records or the continued existence of the resource.

section.name: Complementary Identification Attributes
section.t: The following attributes have complementary roles when describing dynamic resources.

section.name: ID
section.t: The attribute identifies an entity in the IDMEFv2 data model. It MUST be populated in accordance with the applicable IDMEFv2 specification.

An IDMEFv2 identifier and a platform-native identifier are different concepts. For example, a Kubernetes pod UID identifies a Kubernetes object instance; it is not a substitute for the IDMEFv2 attribute. Implementations that need to correlate multiple alerts concerning the same resource SHOULD define a consistent mapping between the resource identity and the IDMEFv2 entity identifier. They SHOULD also distinguish successive resource instances when a platform reuses an operational name.
The identifier MUST NOT be assumed to provide access to a resource or to its historical metadata after termination.

section.name: IP
section.t: The attribute records the network address associated with the entity in the context of the event.

It supports correlation with network telemetry, firewall logs, flow records, and other security monitoring data. However, an IP address is a time-dependent network attribute and MUST NOT be treated as a persistent identifier of an dynamic resource.
When available, the event timestamp and relevant network context SHOULD be retained to support the interpretation of the address at the time of the incident.

Implementations SHOULD distinguish addresses belonging to different infrastructure layers, such as a pod, container, node, NAT gateway, or proxy, when this distinction is relevant to the investigation.

section.name: Hostname
section.t: The attribute records the hostname observed or configured for the entity. It SHOULD contain an actual hostname, not an unrelated platform identifier.

For a Kubernetes pod, the hostname can be configured through the pod's hostname settings or obtained from the runtime environment. A pod name and the hostname used inside the pod may happen to be the same, but they are not interchangeable by definition. Implementations SHOULD record the actual hostname observed or configured for the pod.

Hostnames can facilitate operational identification and correlation during a resource's lifetime. However, hostnames may be reused, and their uniqueness may be limited to a particular namespace, cluster, runtime, or time interval. Consequently, SHOULD NOT be considered a globally unique or permanently stable identifier without additional context.

section.name: Locator
section.t: The attribute can carry a platform-specific resource reference that provides additional context for identifying an entity within its infrastructure.

Depending on the environment, this reference MAY contain a cloud resource identifier, an orchestration resource path, a container identifier qualified by its runtime, or a combination of identifiers that uniquely identifies the relevant resource within its scope.
Implementations SHOULD prefer references that identify the individual resource involved in the event rather than only its parent cluster, service, or workload definition.
Where appropriate, a reference MAY include additional context, such as a cluster identifier, namespace, node identifier, container identifier, or resource UID.
Implementations using platform-specific references SHOULD document their syntax, scope, uniqueness properties, and interpretation.

A value does not, by itself, guarantee that a terminated resource can be retrieved or that its historical metadata remains available. Systems requiring post-incident traceability MUST retain the relevant historical metadata and security telemetry for the required investigation period.

The values are illustrative and MUST be replaced with identifiers and hostnames obtained from the relevant platform in an actual deployment. UUID-shaped values shown in the examples are illustrative IDMEFv2 entity identifiers; they are not Kubernetes UIDs unless explicitly placed in a platform reference.

section.name: Kubernetes
section.t: In Kubernetes, a pod name alone may not be sufficient to distinguish successive instances that share the same name. The pod UID SHOULD be retained when available.
A reference SHOULD include the cluster context, namespace, pod name, and pod UID. Container-specific information MAY be added when the investigation concerns an individual container.

section.name: Docker and Podman
section.t: For standalone container runtimes such as Docker and Podman, a container name alone may be insufficient because names can be reused after a container is removed.
SHOULD identify the container instance and, where necessary, the runtime host or engine. The full container identifier SHOULD be preferred over the human-readable container name.

Implementations SHOULD document whether the reference identifies the container, the runtime instance, the host, or a combination of these entities.
Where multiple runtime hosts or engines are involved, the reference SHOULD include enough context to avoid ambiguity.

section.name: Google Cloud GKE
section.t: For Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), a reference can combine the Google Cloud project and cluster context with the Kubernetes namespace, pod name, and pod UID.
The cluster resource identifier alone identifies the cluster, not the individual pod involved in the incident.
Example:

The scheme is an illustrative convention rather than an official Google Cloud resource URI format. Implementations MAY instead use a documented Google Cloud resource identifier together with the Kubernetes identifiers required to identify the individual pod.

section.name: AWS ECS
section.t: In Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS), the task ARN identifies a task instance, whereas the task definition ARN identifies a versioned task definition.

For incident investigation involving a particular running or terminated task, SHOULD identify the task instance rather than only its task definition. The task definition ARN MAY be retained separately as supplementary configuration context.
Example:

When the incident concerns an individual container within a task, the relevant container identifier SHOULD also be retained when available.

The task definition ARN MAY be recorded as additional information to identify the configuration used by the task. It MUST NOT be substituted for the task instance identifier when the objective is to distinguish individual task executions.

section.name: Microsoft Azure AKS
section.t: In Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), the Azure Resource Manager (ARM) resource ID of a managed cluster identifies the cluster, not an individual pod.
A pod-level reference SHOULD therefore combine the Azure subscription, resource group, and cluster context with the Kubernetes namespace, pod name, and pod UID.

Implementations MAY retain the cluster ARM resource ID as a separate reference or incorporate it into a documented platform-specific representation. The reference SHOULD distinguish the individual Kubernetes resource from its parent cluster.

section.name: HashiCorp Nomad
section.t: In HashiCorp Nomad, an allocation identifier can provide a reference to a particular workload allocation. The reference SHOULD include sufficient context to distinguish allocations across clusters, regions, namespaces, or jobs, as applicable.
Example:

Task-level or container-level information MAY be included when necessary to distinguish the specific runtime entity involved in the event.

section.name: Scope of the Service Attribute
section.t: The attribute in the class SHOULD describe the high-level service or process affected, consistently with the IDMEFv2 specification.
For example, values such as , , and can identify business-level services associated with the target.
Where business services and technical runtime services must be distinguished, implementations SHOULD document the mapping between these concepts and the relevant IDMEFv2 attributes.
The use of for a particular purpose MUST remain consistent with the attribute definition in the applicable version of the IDMEFv2 specification.

section.name: Temporal Context and Historical Retention
section.t: Reliable post-incident investigation requires more than a stable resource reference.

Implementations SHOULD preserve the event timestamp and sufficient contextual information to determine which resource instance, network address, and runtime environment were involved at the time of the event.

The IDMEFv2 time attributes SHOULD be used according to their defined semantics. In particular, indicates when the alert was created, whereas describes the start of the activity or situation being reported when that information is available. They are not interchangeable, and neither should be assumed to represent the exact measurement time of every individual attribute. Implementations SHOULD retain any additional timestamps required to interpret time-sensitive measurements accurately.

Systems requiring long-term traceability MUST retain the historical metadata and security telemetry needed for the intended investigation period. Such information can include orchestration events, container lifecycle records, cloud audit logs, network flow records, and mappings between resource identifiers and network addresses.

A value MAY be used as a lookup key into retained historical records. However, the availability and retention of those records are properties of the surrounding monitoring and logging infrastructure, not guarantees provided by the attribute itself.

section.name: Summary
section.t: Ephemeral environments require a distinction between entity identification, network correlation, and historical resource context.

The attribute identifies the entity in the IDMEFv2 data model. records the network address observed in the context of the event, provides the actual configured or observed hostname, and can carry a platform-specific reference to the relevant resource.

Implementations SHOULD use resource references that identify individual instances rather than only their parent clusters or configuration definitions. They SHOULD preserve sufficient temporal and infrastructure context to distinguish successive instances and correlate events across security telemetry sources.
Long-term traceability additionally depends on the retention and availability of historical metadata and security records.

This approach enables IDMEFv2 to represent dynamic resources across different orchestration platforms and container runtimes without requiring a separate IDMEFv2 extension for each environment. Platform-specific reference formats remain implementation conventions and SHOULD be documented to support interoperability.
The JSON fragments are illustrative. Their exact structure MUST conform to the applicable IDMEFv2 serialization and schema.

section.name: IDMEFv2 Alert Signature Specification
section.t: Proposal
October 2026

This appendix defines a standardized mechanism for signing IDMEFv2 alerts. The signature ensures the integrity and authenticity of alert data while allowing certain attributes to remain modifiable without invalidating the signature (partial signing).
The mechanism builds upon the following standards:

li.t: JWS (RFC 7515) — signature format;
JCS (RFC 8785) — JSON canonicalization;
JWA (RFC 7518) — cryptographic algorithms;
JWK (RFC 7517) — key representation;
IDMEFv2 Paths (Section 3.3.12 of the draft) — attribute selection.

section.t: The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY and RECOMMENDED are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

section.name: Overview
section.t: The mechanism adds two optional attributes to the class:

li.t: ``SignedAttributes``: a list of IDMEFv2 paths identifying the attributes to be signed;
``Signature``: a string containing the JWS Compact Serialization of the signature.

section.t: The signing process follows these steps:

li.t: populate with the list of IDMEFv2 paths;
build the signed payload object as defined in Signed Attributes and Payload Construction;
canonicalize this object using JCS (RFC 8785);
build the protected JWS header (containing , and optionally );
produce the JWS Compact Serialization as defined in ;
store the result in the attribute.

section.name: Signature Format: JWS Compact Serialization
section.t: The attribute MUST use the JWS Compact Serialization format defined in RFC 7515.

section.name: Structure
section.sourcecode: BASE64URL(JWS Protected Header) "." BASE64URL(JWS Payload) "." BASE64URL(JWS Signature)
section.t: The JWS payload MUST be embedded (not detached) in the Compact serialization. It corresponds to the canonicalized representation of the payload object defined in Signed Attributes and Payload Construction, encoded in base64url as specified by RFC 7515.

blockquote.t: Note: The payload is derived from the alert itself; embedding it guarantees that the verifier has access to the exact representation that was signed, independently of any re-serialization of the alert. The unencoded payload option of RFC 7797 is not used.

section.name: Protected Header
section.t: The protected JWS header MUST contain the parameter. It SHOULD contain the parameter. It MUST NOT contain any parameter not specified by this annex.

section.name: Example
section.sourcecode: "Signature": "<valid JWS Compact string, to be provided in test vectors>"

section.name: Path Syntax
section.t: Attributes to be signed are identified using the IDMEFv2 path syntax defined in Section 3.3.12 of the draft.

section.name: Payload Structure (Normative)
section.t: The signed payload MUST be a JSON object whose structure mirrors the nesting of the paths listed in . Specifically:

li.t: a top-level path produces a key at the root;
a nested path produces an object containing a key ;
list indices MUST be contiguous starting from 0 in the payload; unreferenced positions MUST NOT be included;
MUST NOT be included in the payload.

section.name: Absent or Invalid Attributes
section.t: If a path listed in does not correspond to any attribute present in the alert, the producer MUST reject the signing operation (validation error). A verifier that observes the absence of a referenced attribute MUST reject the signature.

li.t: MUST NOT contain or .
The order of paths in the list is not significant (see Attribute Order: Not Significant).
The list MUST be included in the payload to bind the signature to the covered set of paths.

section.name: Attributes Added to the Alert Class

td.t: List of IDMEFv2 paths of the attributes included in the signature.
JWS Compact Serialization string containing the signature.

section.name: SignedAttributes
section.t: Optional. MUST be present when is present. MUST be included in the JWS payload (see Payload Structure (Normative)).

section.name: Signature
section.t: Optional. Present only when the alert is signed. Contains the complete JWS Compact Serialization.

section.name: Consistency
section.t: An alert that contains without , or vice versa, MUST be considered invalid by a verifier.

section.name: Attribute Order: Not Significant
section.t: The order of attributes in does not affect the signature because:

li.t: the payload is canonicalized using JCS (RFC 8785);
JCS deterministically sorts all keys in lexicographic order;
the same logical object therefore always produces the same canonical representation.
Note: The array in the payload preserves the order of the specified indices; JCS does not reorder array elements.

section.name: Normalization: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)
section.t: All JSON objects used as the JWS payload MUST be canonicalized using JCS (RFC 8785) before signing and before verification.

li.t: object keys are sorted lexicographically;
whitespace outside string literals is removed;
numbers are formatted according to I-JSON rules (RFC 7493);
, and are forbidden.

section.name: Rationale
section.t: Without canonicalization, the same logical JSON object could be represented differently (key ordering, whitespace), leading to signature verification failures. JCS ensures deterministic serialization.

section.t: The following algorithms MUST be supported:

section.name: Excluded Algorithms
section.t: The following algorithms MUST NOT be used:

li.t: (unsecured);
, , (HMAC — inappropriate for third-party verification);
any algorithm not listed in JWA (RFC 7518).

section.name: Verification Policy
section.t: A verifier MUST check that the value of the protected header corresponds to an algorithm allowed by its local policy, and MUST reject the signature otherwise (protection against algorithm confusion).

section.name: Key Identification
section.t: ``alg`` parameter. MUST be included in the protected JWS header. It identifies the cryptographic algorithm used to secure the JWS. The signature is not valid if does not represent a supported algorithm, or if no key associated with the signing party is available for that algorithm. The value MUST be a case-sensitive string containing a registered algorithm name (from the IANA "JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms" registry as defined in JWA) or a value that contains a Collision-Resistant Name.

``kid`` parameter. SHOULD be included in the protected JWS header. It provides a hint indicating which key was used to secure the JWS, allowing the recipient to locate the verification key and facilitating key rotation. Other identification mechanisms (out-of-band agreement) MAY be used, which is why this parameter remains optional.
Example header:

section.name: Key Representation
section.t: Keys SHOULD be represented in JWK format (RFC 7517) when exchanged as part of the payload. Other mechanisms, such as referencing a key via a understood within a pre-existing PKI, MAY be used to maintain compatibility with existing infrastructures.

section.name: Key Distribution
section.t: The key distribution mechanism is outside the scope of this annex. The following methods MAY be used: pre-shared public keys, PKI / X.509 certificates, OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect metadata endpoints, manual exchange.

section.name: Verification Procedure
section.t: A verifier MUST apply the following steps:

li.t: check for the joint presence of and (Consistency); reject otherwise;
decode the JWS Compact serialization and check that it has exactly three segments;
check that the protected header contains and that its value is allowed by the local policy (Verification Policy); reject otherwise;
locate the verification key using or another mechanism (Key Management);
canonicalize this object with JCS and compare the result with the decoded payload; reject on any difference;
verify the cryptographic signature using the identified key and algorithm; reject on failure;
on success, consider as intact and authentic only the attributes listed in .
Note: An alert whose and have been removed becomes an unsigned alert. Recipients SHOULD apply an explicit policy (rejection or marking) to unsigned alerts when a signature is expected.

section.name: Key Protection
section.t: Private keys MUST be protected against unauthorized access. Implementations SHOULD use hardware security modules (HSM) or secure enclaves for key storage.

section.name: Algorithm Agility
section.t: To ensure the long-term security of IDMEFv2 alerts, implementations SHOULD support algorithm agility, allowing migration to newer algorithms as cryptographic best practices evolve. As post-quantum signature algorithms (for example ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) are standardized and become widely available, they MAY be used in place of, or in combination with, classical algorithms (for example via hybrid signatures). The parameter facilitates this transition by enabling different key types to be identified without changing the IDMEFv2 data model.

section.name: Replay Attacks
section.t: JWS does not inherently prevent replay attacks. Implementations SHOULD include time-based attributes among the signed attributes (for example ) and/or rely on transport-layer security. The use of JWT-like / claims is outside the scope of the IDMEFv2 model and MUST NOT be assumed by a generic verifier.

section.name: Key Rotation
section.t: Regular key rotation SHOULD be implemented. The parameter facilitates it by allowing the recipient to identify the key used.

Note: ``Confidence`` and ``Analyzer.IP`` do not appear in the payload because they are not listed in ``SignedAttributes``. Signed and verifiable test vectors **MUST** accompany the final version.

section.name: Conformance and Test Vectors
section.t: An implementation is conformant with this annex if it satisfies all the MUST and MUST NOT requirements above. The final version MUST provide:

li.t: at least one test vector per supported algorithm (Supported Algorithms);
one negative test vector per rejection case (Absent or Invalid Attributes, Consistency, Verification Policy, Verification Procedure);
